name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
title: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
answer: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of turning a written question, such as 'which cohort had the highest retention last quarter', into a structured query or analytical routine over a dataset. It sits inside quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the goal is not only to get an answer but to preserve the question, the generated code, and the result for later inspection. The area includes text to SQL, semantic parsing over tables, retrieval over data dictionaries, and conversational follow up questions. It is aimed at analysts, researchers, and domain experts who can describe what they want without writing SQL, Python, or a formal query language.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of turning a written question, such as 'which cohort had the highest retention last quarter', into a structured query or analytical routine over a dataset. It sits inside quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the goal is not only to get an answer but to preserve the question, the generated code, and the result for later inspection. The area includes text to SQL, semantic parsing over tables, retrieval over data dictionaries, and conversational follow up questions. It is aimed at analysts, researchers, and domain experts who can describe what they want without writing SQL, Python, or a formal query language.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work typically runs on a large language model that is given access to a database schema, table descriptions, sample rows, and sometimes a semantic layer that maps business terms to columns. The model may be hosted through an API or run locally, and it is connected to a query engine such as a SQL database, a dataframe library, or a warehouse. A retrieval step often pulls the most relevant tables, columns, and documentation before the model writes a query. The generated query is then executed in a sandboxed or read only environment, and the results are passed back to the model for a plain language summary.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common method starts by grounding the model in the schema and a small set of example question and query pairs. The model proposes a query, which is checked for syntax, table and column names, and row level permissions before execution. If the result is empty, too large, or implausible, the system may ask a clarifying question or revise the query. The final answer includes the plain language question, the generated code, the returned data, and a short explanation, so the work can be reproduced. Iterative refinement is common, with the user correcting a wrong join or filter and the system learning from that correction within the session.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are that a plain language question is ambiguous, that the model hallucinates a column or a join, or that the generated query returns data the user is not allowed to see. Access control is therefore enforced at the database or warehouse layer, not by the language model, and every generated query is logged with the user, timestamp, and source prompt. Provenance matters because a wrong answer can look confident, and the system typically shows the exact query and the rows that produced the result. Privacy and data residency rules apply to the prompt, the schema, and any sample rows sent to a hosted model, and many teams keep those inputs inside their own environment.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more reliable semantic layers that keep business definitions in one place and reduce the chance of a model guessing a column meaning. Agentic workflows are emerging that break a complex question into several queries, run them in sequence, and reconcile the results before answering. Smaller models fine tuned on a team's own schema and query history are becoming practical for on premises use. The plain language interface is likely to become a standard part of reproducible notebooks, with the question, code, and data versioned together. Human review will remain important for high stakes numbers, but the review will shift from writing code to checking the generated query and its assumptions.
